Last verified: 2026-09-28 against AWS documentation.

Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance

This is the exam's center of gravity: 31 percent of the score, roughly 20 scored questions. The domain answers one big question: how do you get the right model, the right data, and the right controls into a working system on AWS? It is the design domain. The other four domains build on it, so a shaky foundation here multiplies everywhere else.

Exam:

AIP-C01

Weight:

31 percent

Questions:

75 total, 65 scored, pass 750/1000

How to use this volume

Every topic reads as one flowing explanation: each fact stated once, every term defined when it first appears, visuals placed at each step with a numbered walkthrough, and exam traps called out where AWS likes to hide them. Read a topic, then do its drill questions at the end. The questions are written in the exam's "choose the MOST correct answer" style, and every answer explains why the right option is right and why each distractor is wrong.

Three ideas run through the whole domain. First, climb the ladder in order: prompt engineering, then RAG, then agents, then fine-tuning. Stop at the cheapest step that works. Second, prefer managed and serverless: the exam rewards the option with the least operational overhead unless a constraint forces custom work. Third, match the tool to the scenario verb: "cite sources" means RAG, "take actions" means agents, "block a topic" means denied topics, "repeated prefix" means caching. Most questions are won by reading the scenario carefully and mapping each constraint to one decision.

1. The approach ladder: prompt, RAG, agents, fine-tuning

The single most-tested judgment call in Domain 1: given a business need, which GenAI approach do you pick, and in which order do you try them?

Think of it as a ladder with four rungs, ordered from cheapest to most expensive. Rung 1, prompt engineering, means changing the instructions and examples you send the model. No new knowledge, no training: you get a new format, tone, or reasoning style. Rung 2, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), means the model looks up facts in your documents at answer time and cites them. Rung 3, agents, means the model can take actions: call APIs, query databases, run multi-step tool use. Rung 4, fine-tuning, means retraining parts of the model on your labeled data so a new behavior is baked into its weights. A cousin of rung 4 is distillation: training a small model to copy a big model, so you get near-big quality at small cost on one narrow task.

The rule: start at the bottom and climb only when the cheaper rung cannot satisfy the requirement. Without this discipline, teams jump straight to the most impressive and most expensive option. A team that fine-tunes because "documents change every quarter" will retrain forever, because the training data is stale the day it ships. A team that builds an agent for "answer questions from our policy PDFs" pays for tool-calling complexity it never needed. Each rung exists for a distinct failure of the rung below: prompting cannot inject new knowledge, RAG cannot take actions, agents cannot bake in a permanent behavior cheaply, and fine-tuning cannot stay fresh.

Turn that into a decision tree with two questions. First: does the model need new knowledge it was not trained on, like company policies or product catalogs? If no, stay with prompt engineering. If yes, ask: do answers need to cite sources or stay current as documents change? If yes, RAG. Next: does the task need actions, like checking a live order status, booking a slot, or querying a database? If yes, agents. Next: does the model need a new baked-in behavior, like a consistent brand voice repeated millions of times, or a small cheap model that matches a big model on one narrow task? If yes, fine-tuning or distillation. If none of these are true, you never left the first rung.

The trap is treating fine-tuning as the "serious" answer and RAG as the "prototype" answer. It is backwards: RAG is the production answer for knowledge problems, because retraining on documents that change quarterly means you are always stale. The exam's favorite wrong answer is "fine-tune the model on the company documents" when the scenario says documents update regularly or answers must cite sources. Fine-tuning also cannot cite sources, because the model cannot point at a page it absorbed during training. If the scenario says "cite sources," the answer is RAG, full stop.

Decision flow: which approach?

  New behavior needed? (brand voice at scale, narrow-task small model)
   YES --> Fine-tune / distill
   NO  |
       v
  Actions needed? (call APIs, query DBs, multi-step tool use)
   YES --> Agents (Bedrock Agents, action groups, session memory)
   NO  |
       v
  New knowledge or citations needed? (docs, policies, current facts)
   YES --> RAG (Bedrock Knowledge Bases, RetrieveAndGenerate)
   NO  |
       v
  New output format, tone, examples, reasoning style?
   YES --> Prompt engineering (system prompt, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
   NO  --> The base model already does it

Cost order of magnitude (illustrative): prompt engineering costs engineering hours only; RAG adds vector storage plus per-query embedding and retrieval cost. An agent call chains several model calls and tool calls per user question, so it can cost 5 to 20 times a single RAG call. Fine-tuning a model on Bedrock needs labeled data in S3 (hundreds to thousands of examples for useful results) plus a customization job and usually Provisioned Throughput to serve it. The exam does not test exact dollars. It tests the relative order: prompt is cheaper than RAG, which is cheaper than agents, which are cheaper than fine-tuning.

  The ladder (climb in order, stop at the cheapest rung that works)

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ RUNG 4: FINE-TUNE      new baked-in behavior, brand voice,  │  most $$$
  │                          narrow-task small model             │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ RUNG 3: AGENTS         actions: call APIs, query DBs,       │
  │                          multi-step tool use, session memory  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ RUNG 2: RAG            new knowledge, current facts,        │
  │                          citations, source attribution        │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ RUNG 1: PROMPT         new format, tone, examples,          │  least $$
  │                          reasoning style. No new knowledge. │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         Climb only when the rung below cannot satisfy the need.

Figure 1.1: The approach ladder. AWS tests whether you climb in order and stop early. Most scenarios never leave rung 1 or 2.

How to read this diagram

  1. Start at the bottom rung, prompt engineering: it changes behavior through instructions only, with no new data and no training.
  2. Climb to RAG only when the model needs knowledge it was not trained on, or answers must cite sources.
  3. Climb to agents only when the task needs actions (API calls, database queries), not just text.
  4. Climb to fine-tuning only when a behavior must be baked into the weights permanently and repeated at scale.
  5. If a component fails the "cheapest rung" test (for example, fine-tuning for documents that change quarterly), the answer is wrong: go back down one rung.

Exam trap. Distractors climb too high ("fine-tune on the documents" for a knowledge question) or too low ("prompt engineering" for a task that needs live API calls). Map each scenario verb to its rung: format/tone is prompt; facts/citations/current is RAG; actions/tools is agents; baked-in behavior at scale is fine-tuning.

How AWS asks this. A 4-6 sentence scenario with a business goal and constraints ("documents updated quarterly", "must cite sources", "same task 10M times a day, cost is the problem"). The right answer is the lowest rung that satisfies every constraint. Distractors each pick the rung above or below.

2. PoC first, the GenAI Lens, and reusable components

How AWS expects you to design before you build: prove it small, check it against the standard lens, and build parts once that every team reuses.

Three design habits. A proof of concept (PoC) is a small throwaway build on Bedrock with on-demand inference that validates feasibility, performance, and business value before any production commitment. The AWS Well-Architected Framework Generative AI Lens is AWS's published checklist for reviewing GenAI workloads across pillars like responsible AI, data, model selection, cost, and security; the exam name-drops it as the standard for "design reviews." Standardized reusable components are the parts you build once and reuse across deployments: prompt templates, model routing layers, guardrail policies, evaluation harnesses.

GenAI projects fail expensively when teams commit to Provisioned Throughput, custom models, or full deployments before knowing the approach works. A PoC on Bedrock costs almost nothing to stand up (on-demand, no infrastructure) and answers the three questions that kill projects: does it work, is it fast enough, is it worth it? The GenAI Lens exists so design reviews are not opinion-based; it gives reviewers a shared checklist. Reusable components exist because every new GenAI feature otherwise reinvents prompt handling, model routing, safety checks, and evaluation, and each reinvention is a new place to fail.

The PoC flow: pick a Bedrock foundation model, run it on-demand (no throughput commitment), wire a minimal RAG or agent loop, measure quality with a small golden dataset, measure latency and token cost, then decide. If the PoC validates, the production design moves through the Lens review: is the data pipeline governed, is model selection justified against cost and latency, are guardrails applied, is there an evaluation gate before each release, is there monitoring? The reusable components that come out of this: a prompt template library (Prompt Management, topic 16), a routing layer that hides model choice behind an internal API (topic 7), a standard guardrail configuration applied to every model call, plus an evaluation harness that every new model version must pass.

A Bedrock PoC can start with zero committed spend: on-demand inference is pay-per-token, and Prompt Management charges nothing extra (you pay only model tokens). A golden dataset for a PoC is typically tens to a few hundred question-answer pairs, enough to spot a failing approach before any throughput commitment. The exam treats "skip the PoC and commit to Provisioned Throughput" as a distractor pattern.

The trap is reading "validate before production" as "write more design documents." The exam means a working PoC on Bedrock with real measurements. Another trap: the GenAI Lens is a review checklist, not a product you deploy; a distractor may say "deploy the GenAI Lens," which is nonsense. A third trap: treating reusable components as optional polish. When a scenario says "five teams building GenAI features" and asks for the most correct architecture, the answer includes shared components (routing layer, guardrail policies, prompt templates), because five bespoke stacks is operational overhead the exam always punishes.

  PoC-first design flow

  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Business │   │ PoC on Bedrock   │   │ GenAI Lens review │
  │  goal +  │──▶│ on-demand, small │──▶│ data, model, cost,│──▶ Production
  │constraints│  │ golden dataset,  │   │ safety, monitoring│   with shared
  └──────────┘   │ measure quality, │   │ pillars checked   │   components
                 │ latency, cost    │   └───────────────────┘   (prompts,
                 └──────────────────┘                           routing,
                     ▲ fails? stop or                          guardrails,
                     │ change approach                         eval harness)
                     └──────────────────────┘

Figure 2.1: Validate small on Bedrock before any commitment. The Lens review is the gate between PoC and production.

How to read this diagram

  1. The business goal and constraints are the input; everything downstream must trace back to them.
  2. The PoC runs on Bedrock on-demand with a small golden dataset; it measures quality, latency, and cost against the constraints.
  3. If the PoC fails, you stop or change approach; you never proceed to commitments like Provisioned Throughput.
  4. The GenAI Lens review checks the design against the standard pillars before production.
  5. Production ships with shared components (prompt templates, routing layer, guardrail policies, evaluation harness) so the next team reuses them instead of rebuilding.

Exam trap. "Select the model with the best published benchmarks" is never a complete answer: benchmarks ignore cost, latency, regional availability, and compliance constraints. Another favorite: training custom models for multilingual support when Bedrock foundation models already cover the needed languages. And EC2 plus load balancer "high availability" only covers one region; it does not answer a failover-across-regions constraint.

How AWS asks this. Scenario: "12 languages, 99.9 percent availability with automatic failover, switch models without code changes, CTO wants validation before production." The correct chain is: PoC on Bedrock, cross-region inference for failover, Lambda plus API Gateway plus AppConfig for model switching, GenAI Lens alignment. Distractors hardcode endpoints, stay single-region, or skip the PoC.

3. Foundation models on Bedrock

The catalog you are choosing from: what each model family is for, and how you get access to call them.

Amazon Bedrock is the fully managed service that lets you call foundation models (FMs) from many providers through one set of AWS APIs, without managing any servers or GPUs. A foundation model is a large model pre-trained on broad data that you use as-is or adapt; you never train it from scratch. Bedrock hosts models from Amazon (Titan, the first-party family for text, embeddings, and image generation; Nova, the newer Amazon family spanning fast cheap models to flagship models, with multimodal variants). It also hosts Anthropic Claude (strong reasoning and long context, a frequent exam default), Meta Llama (open-weights, good for cost-sensitive and customizable deployments), Mistral AI (efficient European models, strong at multilingual and code tasks), and Cohere (strong at multilingual, search, and embeddings). One API surface, many providers: that is the whole point.

Before Bedrock, using a model meant either calling a third-party API (your data leaves AWS, different auth, different contract per vendor) or self-hosting open models on GPUs (capacity planning, patching, scaling). Bedrock gives you one IAM-controlled, VPC-capable, CloudTrail-logged front door to many models. For the exam, this matters because the "most correct" architecture almost always routes through Bedrock rather than a direct vendor API or a self-hosted endpoint, unless the scenario explicitly needs something Bedrock cannot do.

Bedrock has two API planes. The control plane (bedrock endpoint) manages resources: models, knowledge bases, agents, guardrails, provisioned throughput. The data plane (bedrock-runtime endpoint) runs inference: InvokeModel, Converse, streaming variants. Before you can call a model, you must request model access in the Bedrock console for your account and region; some models also require submitting use-case details. Access is per model, per region, per account, and there is no charge to enable it. Once granted, your IAM principal needs bedrock:InvokeModel (or the Converse equivalent) permission, ideally scoped to specific model ARNs. The request then flows: your code, IAM authorization, the runtime endpoint, the provider's model, and the response back, with usage logged for billing.

Bedrock regions each publish a supported-model list, and availability differs: a model available in us-east-1 may not exist in eu-west-1, which is exactly why cross-region inference profiles exist (topic 6). Context windows are model-specific and measured in tokens; flagship models handle hundreds of thousands of tokens, small fast models handle tens of thousands. The exam tests the principle (bigger context is not always better; you pay per token) more than exact numbers.

The trap is assuming every model is available in every region the moment you need it. The exam loves the scenario "model X is only available in two regions, and the application needs resilience": the answer is a cross-region inference profile, not "deploy in more regions" (you cannot deploy a Bedrock model; AWS hosts it). Another trap: AccessDeniedException on a model call usually means model access was never requested or the model is not available in that region, not that your IAM policy is wrong. Check access first.

How to read this diagram

  1. The central box is Amazon Bedrock: the managed service you talk to.
  2. The surrounding boxes are model families from different providers: Amazon Titan and Nova, Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Mistral, Cohere.
  3. Each line is an integration you do not have to build: AWS maintains the provider connection, you just call the model ID.
  4. What breaks if a link fails: if you have not requested access for a model, or it is not available in your region, calls to that box fail with access errors.

Exam trap. Scenarios that ask for "the best model" with no constraints are testing whether you push back: selection needs cost, latency, context, and regional availability constraints (topic 4). Also watch for "self-host Llama on EC2 for full control" as a distractor when Bedrock already serves Llama as a managed model; the exam prefers managed unless a constraint forces self-hosting.

How AWS asks this. "The team needs Claude for reasoning and Titan Embeddings for search, with one auth model and one audit trail." The answer is Bedrock: request access for both models, scope IAM to the two model ARNs, call both through bedrock-runtime. The distractor is calling each provider's own API directly.

4. Choosing the right model

Model selection is a trade-off across five axes. The exam tests whether you can hold all five in your head at once.

Judge every candidate model on five axes: capability (can it do the task well: reasoning, multilingual, code, vision), cost per token (input and output prices differ), latency (time to first token and tokens per second), context window (how much text fits in one call), and regional availability (is it offered where you run). Smaller models (Claude Haiku, Llama 8B, Nova Lite/Micro class) win on cost and latency; flagship models (Claude Sonnet/Opus class, Nova Pro class) win on complex reasoning. There is no universally best model, only the best fit for the constraints.

Picking on capability alone burns money: a flagship model summarizing support tickets costs many times what a small model costs for the same output quality. Picking on cost alone fails tasks: a tiny model cannot do multi-step reasoning over a 200-page contract. The five-axis trade-off exists because real workloads have hard constraints on at least two axes at once, like "sub-second responses in the EU for a multilingual summarizer," and the exam writes scenarios exactly that way.

Selection is a filtering process. First filter by capability floor: run the task on candidate models with a golden dataset (a fixed set of question-answer pairs used as a quality benchmark) and drop anything below the quality bar. Second filter by regional availability: drop models not offered in your region, or add a cross-region inference profile (topic 6) if the model is worth it. Third, rank survivors by cost and latency: measure tokens per request and time to first token on realistic inputs. Fourth, check context window against your longest realistic input plus expected output; if it does not fit, you need chunking, summarization, or a bigger window. The survivor with the lowest cost that clears every bar wins. Revisit the choice quarterly: model prices and capabilities move.

Selection filters (apply in order):

  Candidates ──▶ capability floor? ──▶ region available? ──▶ cost + latency
     │                │ NO: drop            │ NO: drop or        │ rank
     │                │                     │ cross-region       │ survivors
     ▼                ▼                     ▼ profile          ▼
  golden         context window         cheapest model
  dataset test   fits longest input?    that clears all bars

How to read this diagram

  1. Start with candidate models and a golden dataset: anything below the quality bar is dropped first, before cost is considered.
  2. Check regional availability next: a model you cannot run where you operate is not an option without a cross-region profile.
  3. Rank the survivors by cost per token and latency on realistic inputs.
  4. Verify the context window fits your longest realistic input plus expected output; if not, you need chunking or a bigger window.
  5. The winner is the cheapest model that clears every bar; revisit the choice when models or prices change.

Price ratios are illustrative but the order is stable: a flagship model typically costs roughly 10 to 20 times more per token than the smallest model in the same family. Time to first token on a small model is often under a second; on a flagship model with a long prompt it can be several seconds. The exam will not ask you to quote prices; it will give you relative facts ("Model A costs 15x Model B, the task is simple classification") and expect you to pick the cheaper model or a cascade.

The trap is "bigger is safer," so teams default to the flagship model for everything. The exam punishes this: for classification, extraction, and simple summarization, the small model usually matches the big one on a golden dataset, and the "most correct" answer picks it or routes by complexity. The opposite trap is picking the cheapest model for a reasoning task and hoping prompt engineering closes the gap; measure on a golden dataset instead of hoping.

Exam trap. Watch for "choose the model with the best published benchmarks" as the entire answer: benchmarks ignore your cost, latency, and region constraints. Also watch for picking a model that is not available in the scenario's region without adding cross-region inference. That is a guaranteed distractor kill.

How AWS asks this. "Millions of simple support-ticket classifications per day, plus a weekly complex contract analysis, EU data residency, tight budget." The answer: small model (Haiku/Llama 8B/Nova Lite class) for the daily volume, flagship for the weekly analysis, EU region or EU inference profile, golden dataset to prove the small model is good enough. Distractors use the flagship for everything or ignore the EU constraint.

5. Calling models: InvokeModel vs Converse vs streaming

Two APIs do the same job with different trade-offs. Picking the wrong one is a classic exam bug.

InvokeModel is the original Bedrock runtime API: you send a provider-specific JSON body and get the provider-specific response. Each provider has its own body format; for Anthropic Claude you must include anthropic_version: "bedrock-2023-05-31" and max_tokens, or the call fails. Converse is the newer unified API: one request shape (modelId, messages, system, inferenceConfig, toolConfig, guardrailConfig) works across providers, with built-in tool use, inline guardrails, prompt caching hooks (cachePoint), and structured output (outputConfig). Streaming variants (ConverseStream, InvokeModelWithResponseStream) return tokens as they are generated instead of waiting for the full answer. Batch inference is the async option: S3 input, S3 output, hours of latency, roughly half the price.

InvokeModel exists because providers have unique features that a unified API cannot express: embeddings, provider-specific sampling controls, image generation parameters. Converse exists because writing a different request body per provider is operational overhead, and cross-provider features like tool use and guardrails need one contract. Streaming exists because users perceive a chat that starts answering in 300 milliseconds as fast even if the full answer takes 10 seconds; without streaming, every answer waits for the last token. Batch exists for non-interactive work where waiting hours is fine and you want the discount.

A Converse call carries: modelId (the model or inference profile ID), messages (the conversation in roles: user and assistant), system (the system prompt), inferenceConfig (maxTokens, temperature, topP), optional toolConfig (tool definitions for function calling), optional guardrailConfig (guardrail identifier, version, and whether to trace), optional cachePoint (marks where prompt caching applies), and additionalModelRequestFields (the escape hatch for provider-specific parameters). An InvokeModel call carries the raw provider body instead; send the wrong shape and you get ValidationException. Streaming returns an event stream of token chunks; your client reassembles them. Batch inference takes a JSONL file in S3, runs the model over every record, and writes results to S3.

Walkthrough: the code below is the canonical boto3 Converse call the exam expects you to recognize. Read it top to bottom. First you build the runtime client. Then you make one converse() call carrying the model ID, a system prompt, one user message, inference settings, and a guardrail attached inline. Then you read the answer out of the response and check why generation stopped.

import boto3

# WHAT: the Bedrock runtime client. All model invocation APIs live here.
# WHY "bedrock-runtime": the control plane ("bedrock") manages models and KBs.
#   The data plane ("bedrock-runtime") runs inference. Wrong client, wrong APIs.
# WHAT BREAKS: the region must be one where the model is enabled. Otherwise you
#   get ValidationException or AccessDeniedException, not a model answer.
client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

# WHAT: one Converse call with a guardrail attached inline.
# WHY each field:
#   - modelId: an inference profile ID (us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-...)
#     enables cross-region routing. A bare model ID pins you to one region.
#   - system: the system prompt, separate from messages. It sets behavior for
#     the whole conversation.
#   - messages: roles are "user" and "assistant" only. Each content block is a
#     dict with "text". Multimodal calls add "image" blocks here.
#   - inferenceConfig: maxTokens caps the OUTPUT length, not the input.
#     temperature 0 makes output deterministic. Higher values add randomness.
#   - guardrailConfig: applies the guardrail to this call. guardrailIdentifier
#     is the guardrail ID. guardrailVersion is "DRAFT" or a version number.
#     trace="enabled" reports which guardrail policy fired, for debugging.
# WHAT BREAKS: setting both temperature and topP is allowed but they interact.
#   The exam expects temperature OR topP, not both. maxTokens too small
#   truncates the answer mid-sentence with stopReason "max_tokens".
response = client.converse(
    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0",
    system=[{"text": "You are a support assistant. Answer only from the provided context."}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the refund window?"}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 500, "temperature": 0},
    guardrailConfig={
        "guardrailIdentifier": "gr-abc123",
        "guardrailVersion": "DRAFT",
        "trace": "enabled",
    },
)

# WHAT: reading the answer. response["output"]["message"]["content"] is a LIST
#   of blocks. Each block has "text" (or "toolUse" for function calling).
# WHY the loop: a response can carry several text blocks. Index [0] only works
#   when you know there is exactly one.
# stopReason tells you why generation ended: "end_turn" (done), "max_tokens"
#   (truncated, raise maxTokens), "guardrail_intervened" (blocked, check trace).
for block in response["output"]["message"]["content"]:
    print(block["text"])
print("stop reason:", response["stopReason"])

The response shape is the exam payload: output.message.content is a list of blocks, and stopReason names why generation ended. guardrail_intervened as a stop reason is the tell that the guardrail blocked the call.

Which API? (the decision matrix)

  Need                    Use
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Same code for Claude,   Converse / ConverseStream
   Llama, Titan + tool use
  Embeddings              InvokeModel only (Converse is text-generation only)
  Provider-specific       InvokeModel (Converse has additionalModelRequestFields
   feature                as escape hatch, but InvokeModel is the safe answer)
  Real-time token         ConverseStream / InvokeModelWithResponseStream,
   streaming to UI        then WebSockets or SSE to the client
  Async, hours OK,        Batch inference (S3 in, S3 out, ~50% cheaper)
   cheapest per token
  Guardrails inline       Converse guardrailConfig, or standalone ApplyGuardrail
   on the call            (works with any model, even non-Bedrock)

How to read this diagram

  1. Read each row as a need-to-answer mapping: find your need in the left column, take the API in the right.
  2. Note the hard boundary: embeddings are InvokeModel-only; Converse cannot do them under any configuration.
  3. Note the escape hatch: Converse covers most cross-provider work, with additionalModelRequestFields for provider-specific extras.
  4. Streaming rows are about perceived latency: tokens appear as generated, though total time is unchanged.
  5. If a row is misread (for example, batch inference for a chat UI), the latency or capability constraint fails immediately.

Batch inference costs roughly 50 percent less per token than on-demand, in exchange for hours of latency. Streaming cuts perceived latency to the first token (often under a second) while total generation time is unchanged. API Gateway, if placed in front of a GenAI API, has payload and timeout limits (documented, and they change), so long streams usually go through WebSockets or stream directly to the client rather than through a REST API proxy.

The big trap: Converse cannot do embeddings. Embeddings need InvokeModel with the embedding model's provider body. The exam will offer Converse as a distractor for an embeddings task. The second trap: assuming guardrails only work with Converse. The standalone ApplyGuardrail API applies guardrails to any text, including output from non-Bedrock models, which is the answer when the scenario says "we call an external model but need AWS guardrails." The third trap: calling invoke_model with a provider body missing required fields (like Claude's anthropic_version) and debugging IAM for an hour; the error is the request shape, not permissions.

Exam trap. "The application bought Provisioned Throughput but still gets throttled; the code calls invoke_model(modelId='anthropic.claude-...')." The code is calling the base on-demand model, not the provisioned model. The fix is to invoke the provisioned model ARN or identifier. Buying capacity and then not routing to it is one of the exam's favorite bugs.

How AWS asks this. "One codebase must call Claude, Llama, and Titan with tool use and guardrails, and stream answers to a web UI." The answer is Converse plus ConverseStream with toolConfig and guardrailConfig. Distractors use InvokeModel with three hand-rolled request bodies, or put guardrails only on the model instead of the call.

6. Inference routing and pricing: profiles, routers, throughput

Three mechanisms the exam deliberately confuses: inference profiles (availability), prompt routers (cost/quality), Provisioned Throughput (reserved capacity).

Cross-region inference profiles route your request to a model in another region when your region cannot serve it, giving resilience and wider availability. You call the profile ID (with prefixes like us., eu., apac., global.) instead of the bare model ID; for Converse you can pass the profile ARN or ID, for InvokeModel you pass the profile ID. Prompt routers (also called model routers) route each prompt to the cheapest model that can handle its complexity: simple prompts go to a small model, hard ones to the flagship. Provisioned Throughput (PT) is reserved capacity: you commit to model units per hour for 1 to 6 months and get guaranteed throughput and stable latency. On-demand is pay-per-token with no commitment. Batch inference is async and roughly half price. Prompt caching makes repeated input prefixes cheaper.

Each mechanism fixes a different pain. Inference profiles exist because models are not available in every region and a single region can have an outage. Without them, "the model is down" means your application is down. Prompt routers exist because sending every prompt to the flagship model wastes money on easy questions. Provisioned Throughput exists because on-demand has quotas and can throttle you at peak. When you have a steady baseline and a latency promise, you need capacity that is yours. Caching exists because many applications resend the same long system prompt or documents on every call, and paying full price to reprocess identical tokens is waste.

With an inference profile, your request hits the profile endpoint in your region. Bedrock routes it across the AWS backbone (encrypted in transit) to a region hosting the model, and quotas are managed at the source region. With a prompt router, a small classifier or heuristic scores each incoming prompt and picks the target model. The application calls the router ID instead of a model ID. With Provisioned Throughput, you create the commitment with CreateProvisionedModelThroughput, then you must invoke the provisioned model ARN, not the base model ID. The classic bug is buying PT and still calling the base model, which keeps throttling on on-demand quotas. With prompt caching, you mark a cachePoint in the Converse request (or cache_control in InvokeModel). The provider caches the prefix, and cache hits bill at a reduced input-token rate. Caches have a TTL (5 minutes default, up to 1 hour on supported models) and minimum token thresholds per model.

How to read this diagram

  1. The staircase starts at on-demand: no commitment, highest per-token flexibility, the right default for spiky or experimental traffic.
  2. Prompt caching is the next step when the same long prefix repeats on every call; it cuts input cost on the repeated part.
  3. Batch is the step for non-interactive work: hours of latency accepted, roughly half the per-token price.
  4. Provisioned Throughput is the step for steady baselines with latency promises: you pay hourly for guaranteed capacity.
  5. The smaller-model step underlies all of them: route easy work to cheap models regardless of pricing mode.
  6. If a component is misread (for example, treating Provisioned Throughput as a cost saver for spiky traffic), the step fails its purpose: PT guarantees capacity, it does not make bursty traffic cheaper.
Do not confuse these three (the exam's favorite triple):

  Mechanism              Solves               You call
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Inference profile      availability /       profile ID like
  (cross-region)         regional failover    us.anthropic.claude-...
  Prompt / model router  cost vs quality      router ID; it picks
                         per prompt           the model per prompt
  Provisioned            guaranteed capacity  the PROVISIONED model
  Throughput             + stable latency     ARN, not the base model

Provisioned Throughput commits run 1 to 6 months and bill per model unit per hour whether you use the capacity or not, which is why spiky traffic on PT wastes money. Batch inference is roughly 50 percent cheaper per token than on-demand. Prompt caching typically needs a minimum prefix length (model-dependent, on the order of a thousand tokens) and the cache TTL is 5 minutes by default with up to 1 hour on supported models; values are documented per model and change, so treat them as current-documented, not exam-memorized.

The triple confusion above is the trap. "Provisioned Throughput" is the answer to "steady baseline, latency guarantee, throttling at peak," never to "spiky traffic, cut costs." "Prompt caching" is the answer to "same long system prompt on every call," never to "guarantee capacity." "Inference profile" is the answer to "model not available in our region" or "need regional failover," never to "route by prompt complexity." A hybrid answer (PT for the predictable baseline, on-demand for peaks) is often the "most correct" option when both patterns appear in one scenario.

Exam trap. Any scenario that says the team "bought Provisioned Throughput but still gets throttled" is testing one bug: the code invokes the base model ID instead of the provisioned model ARN. Increasing model units does not fix routing. Read the code snippet in the scenario before you touch capacity.

How AWS asks this. "2M requests a day baseline plus 10x Friday spikes, sub-3s latency." The most correct answer is hybrid: Provisioned Throughput for the baseline, on-demand for spikes, often with a smaller model for simple queries. "Entirely SageMaker with GPU autoscaling" fails on cost and cold starts; "fixed EC2 for peak" fails on cost.

7. Swapping models without redeploys

Operations wants to switch between Claude, Titan, and Llama without a code deployment. Here is the canonical AWS answer.

The pattern is three services. AWS AppConfig holds the model choice as runtime configuration: a feature flag or config value like active_model = us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-... that you can change in seconds with validation and gradual rollout. AWS Lambda holds the routing logic: it reads the current config and calls the chosen model through the Converse API. API Gateway is the stable front door: one endpoint for clients, with throttling and usage plans, unchanged no matter which model is behind it. Together they let operations switch models, roll back a bad model, or run A/B tests with zero deployments.

Hardcoding a model ID in application code makes every model change a deployment: build, test, deploy, rollback plan. Model changes are frequent (new versions, price changes, a provider outage, a better small model), and deployments are risky and slow. Externalizing the choice to AppConfig turns a deployment into a config change with validation rules and automatic rollback on bad values. The exam treats "no code changes" and "no redeploy" as hard constraints, and only this pattern satisfies them cleanly.

AppConfig stores a configuration document (JSON or YAML) with the active model identifier, plus optional per-route overrides and rollout strategy. The Lambda function fetches the config at startup and polls or receives updates; on each request it reads active_model and calls Converse with that modelId, because Converse works across providers with one request shape. API Gateway fronts the Lambda with a fixed URL, throttling rules, and API keys per client. For resilience, add a circuit breaker: the Lambda (or a Step Functions wrapper) watches for repeated model errors and temporarily routes to a fallback model or a cached response, then probes the primary before switching back. That is graceful degradation: the system gets cheaper or simpler under failure instead of dying.

AppConfig configuration changes propagate in seconds and support validation lambdas plus deployment strategies (all-at-once, linear, canary) with automatic rollback. API Gateway throttling is configured per route and per usage plan, which protects the model endpoint from client bursts. A circuit breaker typically trips after a small number of consecutive failures (illustrative: 5 failures in a minute) and half-opens after a cooldown to probe recovery.

The trap is reaching for the wrong config store. CloudFormation changes are deployments: using a CloudFormation parameter for the model ID violates "no redeploy" because updating it redeploys the stack. EventBridge routes events. It does not hold configuration, so "store the model choice in EventBridge" is nonsense. Environment variables need a redeploy to change on most compute. AppConfig is the exam's favorite "no redeploy" mechanism. When you see those words, think AppConfig.

  Client ──▶ API Gateway (stable URL, throttling)
                  │
                  ▼
             Lambda (routing logic)
                  │  reads
                  ▼
             AppConfig: { "active_model": "us.anthropic.claude-...",
                          "fallback_model": "amazon.nova-lite-..." }
                  │
                  ▼
             Bedrock Converse ──▶ active model
                  │  on repeated errors: circuit breaker
                  ▼
             fallback model or cached response (graceful degradation)

How to read this diagram

  1. The client only ever sees the API Gateway URL: it never changes, no matter what happens behind it.
  2. Lambda is the routing brain: it reads the active model from AppConfig on each request and calls it through Converse.
  3. AppConfig is the control plane for the choice: operations edits a config value, with validation and rollback, and no code deploys.
  4. Bedrock serves whichever model is active; the circuit breaker watches for repeated errors.
  5. On failure, traffic degrades to the fallback model or cached responses instead of dying, and the breaker probes the primary before restoring it.

Exam trap. The select-three version of this question lists AppConfig, API Gateway, and Lambda as the correct trio. Distractors swap in CloudFormation ("redeploys"), EventBridge ("routes events, holds no config"), or hardcoded model IDs ("needs a deployment to change"). Also: Step Functions is the answer for orchestration with waits and approvals, not for per-request model routing; Lambda does that.

How AWS asks this. "Operations must switch between Claude, Titan, and Llama without code deployments, and the endpoint URL must never change." Select-three: AppConfig plus API Gateway plus Lambda. A second common framing adds "if the primary model fails, fall back automatically": add the circuit breaker and fallback model to the same pattern.

8. Custom models: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, distillation, imports

When the ladder says "bake it into the weights," these are the Bedrock customization options and what each one is for.

Bedrock custom models adapt a foundation model with your data. Fine-tuning (supervised fine-tuning) trains the model on labeled prompt-and-response pairs in S3 so it learns a behavior: a support tone, a classification task, a response format. Continued pre-training trains further on unlabeled domain text (manuals, papers) so the model absorbs domain knowledge and vocabulary. Distillation trains a small, fast, cheap student model to imitate a large teacher model on your task, so you get near-teacher quality at student cost. Imported models let you bring a model you customized elsewhere (for example, a fine-tuned open model) into Bedrock to serve it through Bedrock APIs. Reinforcement fine-tuning exists for tuning with feedback signals. On the SageMaker side, the same ideas appear as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): a parameter-efficient method that trains only small weight deltas (adapters) instead of all weights, then versions them in the SageMaker Model Registry with deployment pipelines and rollback.

Prompt engineering has limits: a 40-page style guide in the system prompt costs tokens on every call and the model still drifts. When a behavior must be consistent across millions of calls, baking it into the weights is cheaper and more reliable than repeating instructions forever. Distillation exists because the best quality often comes from a big model you cannot afford to run at scale; the student gives you the economics. Continued pre-training exists for domains with heavy jargon (legal, medical, engineering) where the base model simply lacks the vocabulary. Imports exist so work done outside Bedrock is not stranded outside Bedrock.

A Bedrock fine-tuning job reads your training and validation files from S3, runs the training, and produces a custom model with its own model ARN. You then serve it: most custom models need Provisioned Throughput to be invocable (some, like Nova custom models, support on-demand). The lifecycle on SageMaker looks like: prepare labeled data, train with LoRA adapters (small and swappable), register the version in Model Registry, deploy through a pipeline with automated tests and rollback, monitor, and retire-and-replace when a better version lands. Imported models skip training: you upload weights in a supported format, Bedrock validates them, and you get a Bedrock model ARN you can call like any other.

Useful fine-tuning typically starts at hundreds to a few thousand high-quality labeled examples; more is better, but quality beats quantity. Training jobs run for hours; you pay for the compute. Serving a custom model usually requires Provisioned Throughput (hourly commit, 1 to 6 month terms), which is why the economics only work when the behavior repeats at scale. LoRA adapters are a small fraction of the full model size, which makes them cheap to store, version, and swap.

The master trap of the whole domain: fine-tuning for knowledge instead of behavior. "Documents updated quarterly" is RAG. "Must cite sources" is RAG. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights that go stale and cannot cite pages. The exam also tests the serving gotcha: a fine-tuned model that is never given Provisioned Throughput (where required) cannot be invoked at all; "the customization job succeeded but calls fail" points at missing throughput, not bad training data. And distillation is the answer to "same narrow task millions of times, cost is the problem," not "we need new knowledge."

  Customization options on Bedrock:

  Need                                    Option
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  New behavior from labeled examples       Fine-tuning (SFT)
   (tone, format, classification)
  Domain vocabulary from unlabeled text    Continued pre-training
  Small cheap model matching a big one     Distillation
   on one narrow task
  Tune with feedback/reward signals        Reinforcement fine-tuning
  Serve a model customized elsewhere       Imported model
  Parameter-efficient training,            LoRA adapters +
   versioned and rolled back               SageMaker Model Registry

How to read this diagram

  1. Each row maps a need to its customization option: match the scenario verb to the left column.
  2. Behavior from labeled examples is fine-tuning; vocabulary from unlabeled text is continued pre-training; they solve different gaps.
  3. Distillation is the economics play: teacher quality at student cost for one narrow repeated task.
  4. Imported models skip training entirely: validate externally trained weights and serve them through Bedrock.
  5. LoRA plus the Model Registry is the SageMaker-flavored lifecycle: small adapters, versioned, deployed with rollback.
  6. If a row is misread (for example, fine-tuning for monthly documents), freshness or citation constraints fail.

Exam trap. Any scenario with "updated quarterly/monthly" plus "fine-tune" in an option is testing whether you reject fine-tuning in favor of RAG with a sync schedule. Any scenario with "millions of repetitions, cost is the problem" plus "RAG" in an option is testing whether you pick distillation or prompt caching instead.

How AWS asks this. "Failed fine-tuned deployment must roll back automatically" points to the SageMaker Model Registry plus a deployment pipeline with rollback. "Consistent brand voice across 50M responses a month, currently enforced with a giant system prompt" points to fine-tuning or distillation to cut the per-call token cost. "Model must answer from documents that change monthly" points away from all of these, to RAG.

9. Data pipelines for FMs: validation, processing, extraction

Models are only as good as the data you feed them. This topic is the ingestion machinery: validate, normalize, extract, format.

Data pipelines for FM consumption do four jobs. Validation checks that incoming data is complete and sane before it reaches a model or a knowledge base: AWS Glue Data Quality runs automated data-quality rules and monitoring, SageMaker Data Wrangler gives a visual interface for data preparation, and custom Lambda functions handle validation and normalization logic. Extraction pulls text and structure out of messy files: Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) processes documents, images, video, and audio into structured output using standard output or custom blueprints; Amazon Transcribe converts audio to text. Enhancement enriches text: Amazon Comprehend extracts entities and detects language or PII, Bedrock itself can reformat text, Lambda normalizes fields. Formatting shapes the final input per model: the Converse API's unified messages format versus InvokeModel's provider-specific bodies, plus JSON schemas for structured output.

Raw enterprise data is hostile to models: scanned PDFs, slide decks, meeting recordings, inconsistent field names, missing values. Feeding that raw into a knowledge base produces a RAG system that retrieves garbage and a model that answers from garbage. Validation exists so bad data is caught at the door with alerts instead of silently poisoning answers. Extraction exists because models read text, not pixels or waveforms; someone must turn the PDF and the call recording into text. Formatting exists because each provider's API expects its own body shape, and a malformed body fails before the model ever sees it.

A typical ingestion pipeline: files land in S3 (with versioning, so you can trace which version of a document produced an answer). An S3 event triggers processing: BDA runs async over documents, images, video, and audio and writes structured results back to S3; Transcribe handles long audio with speaker labels; Lambda validates and normalizes the extracted fields; Comprehend adds entities or flags PII; Glue Data Quality monitors the pipeline's outputs with rules and publishes CloudWatch metrics for observability. The cleaned records then feed a knowledge base sync or a fine-tuning dataset. BDA offers standard output (predefined schemas per modality) versus custom blueprints (you define the fields to extract); async jobs write results to S3 when done.

BDA handles four modalities (documents, images, video, audio) in one service and runs asynchronously. Large video files take minutes to process. Knowledge base data sources have documented file size limits (on the order of tens of MB per file; verify current docs at build time). Transcribe supports speaker diarization and custom vocabularies for domain terms. The exam cares about which service does which job, not the exact limits.

Two big traps. First, Bedrock Guardrails do not extract content: Guardrails are safety filters, and the exam offers them as a distractor for extraction tasks. Extraction is BDA, Transcribe, or Comprehend. Second, Amazon Kendra is not a knowledge base: Kendra is enterprise search (it finds documents), while Bedrock Knowledge Bases do RAG (retrieve plus generate with citations). The exam swaps them: "we need generated answers with citations" is Knowledge Bases, not Kendra.

How to read this diagram

  1. Trace the left edge: raw data sources feed into the ingestion layer; S3 is the durable landing zone.
  2. Follow the processing stage: extraction and transformation services turn raw files into structured, validated records.
  3. Note the storage layer in the middle: versioned, queryable stores that downstream GenAI services read from.
  4. Trace right: consumers (agents, knowledge bases, analytics) read the processed data, never the raw files.
  5. If a component fails: no versioning means you cannot trace which document version produced an answer; no validation means bad data flows silently into retrieval.

Exam trap. "Ingest 10,000 mixed files a day (PDF, PPT, video) and extract key concepts into structured summaries." The answer chains Bedrock Data Automation (blueprints, standard versus custom output) plus S3 versioning. Distractors use Guardrails for extraction (wrong tool) or Neptune for the extracted text (Neptune is a graph store for GraphRAG relationships, not a document store).

How AWS asks this. Multimodal ingestion scenarios always resolve to BDA for extraction, Lambda for validation and normalization, Glue Data Quality plus CloudWatch for monitoring. If the scenario mentions audio specifically, Transcribe appears in the correct chain. Formatting questions test Converse (unified messages) versus InvokeModel (provider bodies) and JSON schema for structured output.

10. Knowledge Bases: the managed RAG service

Bedrock Knowledge Bases turn your documents into a queryable RAG backend with almost no code. This is the service behind half the exam's RAG questions.

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG service. You connect data sources: S3 buckets, a web crawler, Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce. The service ingests the documents, chunks them (topic 13), embeds them (topic 14), and stores the vectors in your chosen vector store (topic 11). You set sync schedules so new and changed documents are picked up automatically. At query time you call Retrieve (get the relevant chunks) or RetrieveAndGenerate (get chunks plus a model-generated answer with source citations) through the bedrock-agent-runtime endpoint. You can also attach a knowledge base to a Bedrock Agent for grounding.

Building RAG by hand means writing the chunker, the embedder, the vector store client, the sync scheduler, the retrieval logic, and the citation plumbing, then operating all of it. Knowledge Bases collapse that into a managed resource: you point at documents and get APIs. For the exam, this is the default answer to any "private documents plus citations" scenario; hand-rolled RAG is a distractor unless the scenario needs something the managed service cannot do (like a custom retrieval algorithm).

Ingestion: each data source has a sync configuration (one-time, scheduled, or on-demand). On sync, the service parses documents (with an optional advanced parsing step for complex layouts and tables), applies the data source's chunking strategy (set at creation; changing it requires recreating the data source), embeds each chunk with the configured embedding model, and upserts vectors plus metadata into the vector store. Retrieval: your query is embedded with the same model, the vector store returns the nearest chunks (optionally with hybrid search and reranking, topic 15), and RetrieveAndGenerate passes those chunks as context to the generation model with an instruction to cite sources. Metadata (S3 object metadata, custom attributes, tags) enables filtered retrieval, for example "only documents tagged region=EU."

The default chunking strategy produces chunks of roughly 300 tokens, which is fine for prototyping and often wrong for production. Chunking is set per data source at creation time. Changing it means recreating the data source and re-ingesting. Sync schedules can be hourly, daily, or custom. "Documents updated quarterly" in a scenario is a direct pointer to configuring a sync schedule rather than doing one-time loads.

The multi-tenant trap: one shared knowledge base for tenants with different access controls is wrong. The exam wants isolation: separate knowledge bases per tenant (or per account) with IAM-scoped access, not one KB plus prompt instructions like "only answer about your own hotel." Prompt-level filtering is not a security boundary. Also: Retrieve versus RetrieveAndGenerate matters; if the scenario needs citations in a generated answer, you need the latter (or you generate yourself from retrieved chunks).

How to read this diagram

  1. Left column: the supported data source types; each can have its own sync schedule.
  2. Center: the Knowledge Base, which chunks, embeds, and indexes everything it ingests.
  3. Right: the vector store holds the embeddings and the retriever serves queries.
  4. The arrows are one-way for ingestion (documents flow in on sync) and the retriever answers queries against what was ingested.
  5. If a component fails: no sync schedule means answers go stale as documents change; the wrong chunking strategy at creation means rebuilding the data source to fix retrieval.

Exam trap. "Each hotel needs separate access controls and near-real-time availability data." The answer is one KB per tenant with IAM boundaries plus direct ingestion for the real-time feed. The distractor is a single shared KB with "the model is instructed to respect tenant boundaries." Instructions are not access control.

How AWS asks this. "Documents updated quarterly, answers must cite sources, minimal operational overhead." The chain is: Knowledge Bases with S3 data source, scheduled sync, RetrieveAndGenerate. The exam will offer Kendra (search, not RAG), hand-rolled OpenSearch pipelines (operational overhead), and fine-tuning (stale, no citations) as distractors.

11. Vector stores compared

Knowledge Bases need somewhere to put the vectors. Each store has a personality; the exam tests the match.

A vector store (also called a vector database) stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones to a query embedding fast. Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports several. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless with vector collections is the managed, scalable default. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector stores vectors alongside relational data, so one database holds both your tables and your embeddings. Amazon Neptune is a graph database; with Knowledge Bases it powers GraphRAG, retrieval over entities and relationships, not just text similarity. Amazon S3 Vectors is the low-cost option for smaller-scale vector workloads and dev/test. Third-party options (Pinecone, MongoDB Atlas, Redis) connect through connectors for teams already invested in them.

Different workloads need different trade-offs. A search over 100M product embeddings needs a scaled vector engine (OpenSearch). An application that already lives in Postgres and needs "find similar support tickets for this customer" wants vectors next to its relational rows (Aurora pgvector) rather than a second database to operate. A fraud or knowledge-graph workload needs to traverse relationships ("which suppliers connect to this part through two hops"), which similarity search cannot do (Neptune). A prototype or small workload should not pay for a scaled cluster (S3 Vectors). The exam frames each store by its best fit, and scenarios are written to match exactly one.

All of them do approximate nearest-neighbor search: given a query vector, return the K closest stored vectors by a distance metric (cosine similarity is typical). OpenSearch Serverless manages sharding and scaling for you. You can run multi-index setups per domain for performance isolation. Aurora pgvector adds a vector column and an index type (IVFFlat or HNSW) to Postgres. Queries combine SQL filters ("customer = X") with vector similarity in one statement, which is its superpower. Neptune stores a knowledge graph (entities as nodes, relationships as edges). GraphRAG traverses the graph to gather connected context, then the model reasons over it. S3 Vectors stores vectors as S3 objects with an index, trading query performance for very low cost and zero cluster management.

Store Best fit Exam signal
OpenSearch Serverless Large-scale vector search, managed, sharded "millions of vectors," "managed," "multi-index per domain"
Aurora PostgreSQL + pgvector Relational data plus vectors in one DB "already on Postgres," "filter by customer then similarity"
Neptune GraphRAG: entities and relationships "relationships," "multi-hop," "knowledge graph"
S3 Vectors Cost-sensitive, smaller scale, dev/test "prototype," "low cost," "small scale"
Pinecone / MongoDB / Redis Team already uses them "existing investment," third-party connector 
  Vector store decision flow:

  Need vectors next to relational rows? ──YES──▶ Aurora pgvector
   NO │
      ▼
  Need multi-hop relationship traversal? ──YES──▶ Neptune (GraphRAG)
   NO │
      ▼
  Team already invested in Pinecone / Mongo / Redis? ──YES──▶ third-party connector
   NO │
      ▼
  Large scale, fully managed? ──YES──▶ OpenSearch Serverless
   NO │
      ▼
  Cost-sensitive prototype or small scale? ──YES──▶ S3 Vectors

  Never: ElastiCache (ephemeral) or DynamoDB (not a vector store)
  as the durable vector home.

Figure 11.1: Match the workload shape to the store. Each question eliminates all but one answer.

How to read this diagram

  1. Start at the top question and answer honestly; the first YES picks your store.
  2. Relational plus vectors in one database is the pgvector signal; relationships and hops are the Neptune signal.
  3. Existing third-party investments are respected through connectors rather than migrations.
  4. Scale and budget decide between OpenSearch Serverless and S3 Vectors.
  5. The bottom line is the trap list: ElastiCache and DynamoDB are never the durable vector home, no matter how plausible they sound.

Embedding dimensions drive storage and cost: Titan Text Embeddings v2 supports 1024, 512, or 256 dimensions (topic 14). Smaller dimensions mean proportionally smaller indexes and faster search at some accuracy cost. OpenSearch Serverless scales compute automatically. Aurora pgvector index choice (HNSW for recall and speed, IVFFlat for build simplicity) is a documented tuning knob. Treat specific scale numbers as illustrative; the exam tests fit, not capacity math.

Three traps. ElastiCache for durable vectors: ElastiCache is a cache. It is ephemeral by design, so vectors live in a real store and ElastiCache holds hot results. DynamoDB as the vector store: DynamoDB is for metadata and session state, not vector similarity search. The exam offers it because "it is fast and serverless," which is true and irrelevant. Neptune for plain document RAG: Neptune earns its place only when the scenario mentions relationships or graph traversal. For plain similarity search it is the expensive wrong answer.

Exam trap. "The application already runs on Aurora PostgreSQL and needs similar-ticket search filtered by customer." The answer is Aurora pgvector: one database, SQL filter plus vector search in one query. Distractors propose a new OpenSearch cluster (extra operational overhead for no reason) or DynamoDB (not a vector store).

How AWS asks this. Scenarios name the workload shape and expect the store: "millions of product embeddings, fully managed" is OpenSearch Serverless; "fraud rings, multi-hop relationships" is Neptune with GraphRAG. "Prototype on a budget" is S3 Vectors. The wrong answers are always a plausible store with the wrong personality.

12. RAG end to end

The full retrieval-augmented generation loop, traced from document to cited answer. This is the architecture behind the most questions in Domain 1.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the pattern where the model does not answer from its training weights alone: at query time, the system retrieves relevant passages from your documents and stuffs them into the prompt as context, then the model answers from that context and cites it. The loop has five stages: ingest (documents in), chunk and embed (split text, turn chunks into vectors), store (vectors plus metadata in a vector store), retrieve (embed the query, find nearest chunks), generate (model answers from the retrieved context with citations). Bedrock Knowledge Bases with RetrieveAndGenerate runs the whole loop managed.

Foundation models have a knowledge cutoff and no access to your private data; they also hallucinate confidently when they do not know something. RAG fixes both without retraining: new documents are searchable the moment they are ingested, and the model is instructed to answer only from the retrieved passages, which it can cite. That is why "documents updated quarterly" and "must cite sources" are RAG signals: fine-tuning cannot do either, and prompt engineering has no new knowledge to work with.

Trace one question, "What is our refund window?", through the loop. Ingest: the returns policy PDF is already synced into the knowledge base. Chunk and embed happened at sync time: the PDF was split into chunks and each chunk became a vector. Retrieve: your question is embedded with the same embedding model; the vector store returns the top-K nearest chunks (say, 5 chunks about refunds and returns). Generate: RetrieveAndGenerate builds a prompt containing your question plus those chunks, with a system instruction like "answer only from the provided sources and cite them"; the model produces "30 days (source: returns-policy.pdf, page 4)." Freshness comes from the sync schedule: changed documents are re-chunked and re-embedded automatically. Metadata filtering narrows retrieval before similarity search ("only policies tagged region=US").

Walkthrough: the code below runs the whole RAG loop managed in one boto3 call. It pairs with the pipeline diagram above. Read it in three steps. Build the agent-runtime client. Call retrieve_and_generate with the question, the knowledge base ID, the answering model, and how many chunks to retrieve. Then print the answer and walk the citations.

import boto3

# WHAT: the client. RetrieveAndGenerate lives on "bedrock-agent-runtime",
#   the same client agents use. It is a data-plane API, not control plane.
# WHAT BREAKS: the "bedrock" (control-plane) client has no retrieve_and_generate
#   method. Calling it there raises AttributeError before any network call.
client = boto3.client("bedrock-agent-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

# WHAT: one call that runs retrieve then generate, fully managed.
# WHY each field:
#   - input.text: the user question. The KB embeds it with the KB's own
#     embedding model, the same one used at ingestion. Mismatched embedding
#     models between ingest and query silently wreck retrieval quality.
#   - type "KNOWLEDGE_BASE": the managed path. ("EXTERNAL_SOURCES" is the
#     bring-your-own-retrieval path.)
#   - knowledgeBaseId: which KB to search. Chunking strategy, embeddings, and
#     vector store were all fixed when the KB was created. This call just queries.
#   - modelArn: the FM that writes the final answer from the retrieved chunks.
#     Must be a full ARN, not a bare model ID.
#   - numberOfResults: top-K chunks stuffed into the prompt. More chunks mean
#     more context tokens, higher cost, slower answers, and diluted relevance.
# WHAT BREAKS: numberOfResults too high floods the prompt with marginal chunks.
#   Too low and the answer misses the key passage. 5 is the sane default.
response = client.retrieve_and_generate(
    input={"text": "What is the refund window?"},
    retrieveAndGenerateConfiguration={
        "type": "KNOWLEDGE_BASE",
        "knowledgeBaseConfiguration": {
            "knowledgeBaseId": "kb-abc123",
            "modelArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0",
            "retrievalConfiguration": {
                "vectorSearchConfiguration": {"numberOfResults": 5}
            },
        },
    },
)

# WHAT: the answer plus its evidence.
# response["output"]["text"] is the final answer string.
# response["citations"] lists every retrieved chunk: the S3 URI it came from
#   and the exact text span used. "Must cite sources" in a stem means RAG,
#   and citations are the mechanism.
# WHY read citations: they are your grounding proof. An answer with no
#   citations usually means the model answered from weights, not your documents.
print(response["output"]["text"])
for citation in response.get("citations", []):
    for ref in citation["retrievedReferences"]:
        print("-", ref["location"]["s3Location"]["uri"])

How to read this diagram

  1. Stage 1, Documents: your private files; they enter through a sync schedule, not a training job.
  2. Stage 2, Embeddings: each chunk becomes a vector; the query will be embedded with the same model.
  3. Stage 3, Vector Store: the durable index of chunk vectors plus metadata.
  4. Stage 4, Retriever: embeds your question and returns the nearest chunks (top-K).
  5. Stage 5, Language Model plus Answer: the model receives question plus chunks and answers with citations.
  6. If a stage fails: bad chunking (stage 2) splits answers across chunks and retrieval misses; stale sync (stage 1) serves old policy. The model ignoring context (stage 5) is a grounding failure, fixed with instructions and grounding checks, not a bigger model.

A typical RetrieveAndGenerate call retrieves the top 5 to 10 chunks; more chunks mean more context tokens and higher cost per answer, so K is a cost lever. Default chunking is roughly 300 tokens per chunk, so 5 chunks add about 1,500 tokens of context to every answer. End-to-end RAG latency is the sum of embedding time plus vector search plus generation; the generation step dominates.

The trap is debugging RAG failures at the wrong stage. "RAG returns confident but wrong answers, and the retrieved chunks look relevant" is a generation/grounding problem (the model is not using the context), not a retrieval problem; the fix is instructions, grounding checks, or structured output, not a new embedding model. "Retrieved chunks are irrelevant" is a retrieval problem (chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, rerank: topic 15). Switching the generation model when retrieval is broken is the exam's favorite wrong fix.

Exam trap. "Tables in our manuals get split across chunks and answers miss the numbers." The answer is advanced parsing plus hierarchical chunking (topic 13), which keeps table context together. The distractor is "switch to a larger generation model," which changes nothing about how tables were split at ingestion.

How AWS asks this. "Customer support answers must cite the policy document and stay current as policies change monthly." The chain is Knowledge Bases with S3 source, monthly sync schedule, RetrieveAndGenerate. The exam offers fine-tuning (stale, no citations), Kendra alone (search without generation), and a bigger model (does not add knowledge) as distractors.

13. Chunking strategies

How you cut documents decides what retrieval can find. This is the most technical corner of Domain 1 and a rich source of scenario questions.

Chunking is splitting documents into pieces before embedding, because embedding models take limited input and retrieval works best on focused passages. Bedrock Knowledge Bases offers strategies set per data source at creation time (changing later means recreating the data source). Default chunking splits into roughly 300-token pieces and is meant for prototyping. Fixed-size chunking splits every N tokens with an overlap percentage, which is predictable. Hierarchical chunking creates two levels: small child chunks for precise matching and larger parent chunks that supply surrounding context at generation time. Semantic chunking splits at meaning boundaries (sentences and topics), which gives the best retrieval quality at higher ingestion cost. None means your documents arrive pre-chunked and the service stores them as-is. Custom chunking uses a Lambda function you write for exotic formats.

Chunking is the lever between two failures. Chunks too large dilute the embedding: a 5,000-token chunk about ten topics matches vaguely on all of them and precisely on none. Chunks too small shatter context: the sentence "the window is 30 days" is useless without knowing it refers to refunds, which lived two chunks away. Overlap exists so a sentence split at a boundary still appears whole in a neighbor. Hierarchical chunking exists for structured documents (manuals, legal contracts, docs with headings): match precisely on the child, then hand the model the parent so it sees the section the sentence came from.

At ingestion, the parser walks each document and applies the strategy. Fixed-size: cut every N tokens, keep the last X percent as overlap into the next chunk. Hierarchical: first cut parents (for example, by section or large token windows), then cut children inside each parent and record the parent-child link; at retrieval, the child matches the query, then the parent's text is what gets passed to the model as context. Semantic: the service analyzes sentence and topic boundaries and cuts where meaning shifts, which costs more compute at ingestion because it runs a model over the text. The strategy plus its parameters are stored on the data source; re-ingestion after a strategy change rebuilds every vector, which is why the choice is sticky.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top row, fixed-size: equal blocks with small overlaps; predictable, cheap, blind to document structure.
  2. Middle row, hierarchical: small child blocks grouped under larger parent blocks; retrieval matches on the child, generation reads the parent.
  3. Bottom row, semantic: uneven blocks that follow sentences and topics; best boundaries, most expensive ingestion.
  4. Compare the failure modes: fixed-size can split a table row across two blocks; hierarchical keeps the section together; semantic keeps the thought together.
  5. The exam maps document type to strategy: structured manuals and legal text point to hierarchical; FAQs tolerate fixed-size; "best quality regardless of cost" points to semantic.
Strategy picker:

  Document type                      Strategy
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Quick prototype, mixed docs        default (~300 tokens)
  FAQs, short uniform passages       fixed-size (+ overlap %)
  Manuals, legal, structured docs    hierarchical (child match, parent context)
  Best quality, cost is secondary    semantic (slower, pricier ingestion)
  Already split upstream             none
  Exotic format (CAD, custom XML)    custom via Lambda

Default chunking is about 300 tokens per chunk. A common fixed-size setup is 500 to 1,000 tokens with 10 to 20 percent overlap; overlap below 10 percent risks losing boundary sentences, above 20 percent wastes storage on duplicated text. Hierarchical setups often use children of 200 to 400 tokens under parents of 1,000 to 2,000 tokens. Semantic chunking can cost several times more at ingestion than fixed-size because it runs analysis over the text; the exam frames this as "best quality, slower and more expensive ingestion."

The trap is "semantic is always best." It is the best quality, but the exam punishes over-engineering: for FAQs and short uniform docs, fixed-size is fine and cheaper, and the "most correct" answer picks the simpler strategy. The opposite trap is fixed-size for structured documents: splitting a contract's clause across chunks breaks retrieval in ways no embedding model can fix, and the exam's preferred answer for manuals and legal text is hierarchical. Also: chunking is set at data-source creation, so "just change the chunking" is never a quick fix; the scenario expects you to know it requires recreating the data source.

Exam trap. "Retrieval misses answers that span section boundaries in our product manuals." The answer is hierarchical chunking. The distractors are "increase the embedding dimensions" (does not fix split context), "switch the generation model" (retrieval problem, not generation), and "use semantic chunking because it is the best" (plausible, but hierarchical is the exam's preferred answer for structured docs).

How AWS asks this. Scenarios name the document type and the failure symptom, and the strategy follows: tables broken across chunks, answers needing section context, FAQs with simple passages. The wrong answers always fix the wrong stage or over-engineer the strategy.

14. Embeddings: Titan Embeddings and Cohere Embed

Embeddings turn text into numbers so "similar meaning" becomes "short distance." Two models dominate the exam.

An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents a piece of text; texts with similar meaning get vectors that sit close together in space. An embedding model does the conversion. On Bedrock, the two exam-relevant choices are Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2, the cheap default with configurable dimensions (1024, 512, or 256), and Cohere Embed, which is strong for multilingual content and takes an input_type parameter distinguishing search_query from search_document so queries and documents are embedded appropriately. You call embedding models with InvokeModel, never Converse, because Converse is text-generation only. The dimension count is the length of the vector: more dimensions capture more nuance but cost more storage and slower search.

Keyword search cannot match "refund window" to "returns period," because the words differ while the meaning matches. Embeddings exist so retrieval works on meaning: the query and every chunk become vectors, and the nearest vectors win regardless of exact words. The dimension choice exists because it is a direct cost lever: halving dimensions roughly halves vector storage and speeds up search, at some accuracy cost that a golden dataset can measure.

At ingestion, each chunk is sent to the embedding model and the returned vector is stored alongside the chunk text and metadata. At query time, the user's question is embedded with the same model and same dimensions; mixing models or dimensions between ingestion and query silently breaks retrieval because the vector spaces do not align. The vector store computes a distance (cosine similarity is typical) between the query vector and stored vectors and returns the nearest K. Cohere's input_type matters because it embeds queries and documents with different prefixes optimized for each role; using the wrong type degrades match quality. Titan v2's configurable dimensions let you pick 256 for cheap large-scale search or 1024 when nuance matters, without changing models.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left side: short texts enter the embedding model and come out as points (vectors).
  2. The plot: each dot is one chunk; distance between dots is meaning distance, not word overlap.
  3. The dashed circles: clusters of related content; a query about one cluster member retrieves its neighbors.
  4. The arrows: the same conversion must be applied to the query at search time, with the same model and dimensions.
  5. If a component fails: mismatched models or dimensions between ingestion and query put the query in the wrong space and retrieval returns nonsense.

Titan Text Embeddings v2 offers 1024, 512, and 256 dimensions; dropping from 1024 to 256 cuts vector storage to a quarter and speeds up search proportionally, with an accuracy trade-off you measure on a golden dataset. Cohere Embed supports 100+ languages, which is why multilingual scenarios point at it. Embedding calls are InvokeModel calls billed per token like any other model input; they are cheap relative to generation, but millions of chunks add up at ingestion.

Three traps. First, calling embeddings through Converse: it cannot do it; embeddings are InvokeModel-only, and the exam offers Converse as the distractor. Second, more dimensions are not automatically better: beyond the point your golden dataset stops improving, extra dimensions are pure cost.
